extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in internet humor and digital culture
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate the characteristics, media, impacts, and functions of humor as it appears and spreads on the Internet (memes, GIFs, short videos, ASCII art, reaction videos, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagation speed and extent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet significantly increased the speed and the extent of the propagation of humor over the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by how rapidly and widely they spread online; the article explicitly compares Internet-era propagation to prior media and includes the rec.humor FAQ vignette illustrating rapid reposting and wide readership (somebody posts a joke → tens of thousands read it → repeated reposting). Consider reach (global vs local) and tempo of spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replicability, sociability, and participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes and other Internet humor 'harness "key logics" of online life: replicability, sociability, and participation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a humorous item is easily copied/repurposed (replicable), whether it fosters social interaction (sociable), and whether audiences can and do become producers (participation). The shift from passive consumption to active creation is a central evaluative dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutation and evolution of jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes and folklore undergo evolution and mutations online; the Internet 'speeds up and globalizes these processes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how an instance of humor changes as it is remixed, localized, or iterated—variants, callbacks, and transformative reuses indicate memetic evolution. The rec.humor FAQ example (loops of reposting and slight changes) is an exemplar of this dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced censorship and spread of taboo/dark humor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet as a whole eliminates censorship and self-censorship of humor; black comedy (e.g., dead baby jokes) that was once spread orally now spreads online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether online platforms enable humor that would be censored or self-censored elsewhere; note ethical and community-norm implications. Also consider how the Internet 'blurred the lines between what is permitted in private and in public.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of shared cultural references as a humor shortcut
rubrics_metrics.description: A core aspect of GIFs' and memes' effectiveness lies in their references to popular media or past events, which 'provide a shortcut for viewers to communicate, understand and connect with the humor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how reliant the humor is on shared background knowledge: stronger, widely-known references increase immediate comprehensibility and resonance but may exclude niche audiences. Evaluate plausibility of recognition across platforms and cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: GIF-specific effectiveness factors
rubrics_metrics.description: GIFs are concise, looping animations whose repetitive nature and references to popular media intensify comedic effect; they frequently include overlaid text/captions and their non-verbal visual nature can transcend language and cultural barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a GIF, consider: brevity and looped repetition (comic timing), choice of reference (recognizability), use of overlaid text to provide context/punchline, and nonverbal expressiveness for cross-cultural reach. The article notes that layering assists viewer comprehension and that looping 'allows the sender and viewer to expect and savor the comic effect.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme form and dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes are typically images with text superimposed which together create a humorous effect; they are associated with participatory creation and often use styles like sarcasm and silliness. They can be niche or go viral and 'unite people through shared interests and humor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate meme pieces by format fidelity (image+text), stylistic choices (sarcasm, silliness), memetic potential (ease of replication and variation), community- or culture-specificity, and political or social footprint (memes are often implicated in political contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-form video characteristics for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-form videos (typically under three minutes) are fast-paced, built around authentic self-expression and audio-visual editing, and tailored to shorter attention spans on platforms like TikTok, YouTube Shorts, and Instagram Reels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess length, pace, editing, authenticity, and platform fit. Consider how well the video captures attention, aligns with audience comedic preferences, and uses audiovisual techniques to deliver punchlines. The article links these qualities to increased engagement and stress-relief effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor's psychological and social effects (engagement, stress relief, persuasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous short-form videos evoke positive emotions, provide stress relief, increase engagement, and have been effective in promoting preventive health behaviors and improving message recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing humorous content, measure intended outcomes: emotional uplift, engagement metrics (likes/comments/shares), behavior-change effectiveness (e.g., public-health uptake), and whether humor reduces defensive reactions. The COVID-19 social distancing videos example illustrates persuasive utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence of new digitally-native humor formats
rubrics_metrics.description: New possibilities of electronic communication produced formats such as ASCII art, lolcats, demotivators, and funny animations; image/video manipulation plus easy dissemination enabled these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty and medium-specific affordances: does the work leverage digital editing/manipulation in ways impossible pre-Internet? Consider ubiquity (e.g., ASCII art in sig blocks) and subgenre conventions (e.g., lolcat image macros).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blurring of written/spoken modes and directness of voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The Internet blurred the lines between written and spoken language use and the directness of speech; platforms like YouTube blur between a spoken and recorded joke because the narrator is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tone and voice: is humor written to imitate speech, or is it clearly performative? Consider how presence of a visible narrator or conversational style affects immediacy, perceived authenticity, and comedic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and creator production skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous short-form videos are often created by a diverse mix of comedians, influencers, and content creators skilled in audio-visual editing; authenticity and self-expression help connect with audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the balance between polished production and perceived authenticity: strong editing can enhance comedic timing, but authentic self-expression often increases audience connection. Consider creator identity, editing quality, and platform conventions.
